tier_reason: The arXiv 2303.09419 v1 preprint measures Cyclone DDS against Kafka 3.2.1 (text, Tab. 2/3 latency, appendix Tab. 4-7 raw throughput) on a stated Ryzen 7 5800X. It states no compiler or flags, its benchmark code (github.com/ZettaScaleLabs/zenoh-perf, comparison/) is now 404, and it is not peer-reviewed (v1 only, no journal-ref, no Crossref venue). It was also run by ZettaScale, then the main Cyclone DDS developer, so this is first-party-leaning, not independent. That makes it C, the same tier the Zenoh entry got from this paper.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Single machine: Cyclone DDS reaches 2.3-2.5M msg/s at 8-16 B vs Kafka's 61.6-62.5K msg/s (~37-40x, derived from page data, Tab. 4); the text says DDS reaches 'up to 2M msg/s' and Kafka holds 53K-62K msg/s below 2 KiB. Bitrate at matched payloads: 23.1 vs 3.6 Gbps at 32 KiB (~6.4x) and 25.8 vs 3.5 Gbps at 256 KiB (~7.4x) (derived from page data, Tab. 5); the text gives a DDS peak of 26 Gbps and has Kafka saturating at ~3-4 Gbps. 64 B ping-pong latency (RTT/2): 8 us vs 73 us (~9x, derived from page data). Multi-machine, 100GbE: 13.9 vs 4.6 Gbps at 32 KiB (~3x) and a DDS max of 14.4 Gbps (derived from page data, Tab. 7; the text says 14 Gbps for DDS and 5 Gbps for Kafka's best). Latency 38 us vs 84 us (~2.2x, derived from page data).
corrections.workload: Pub/sub throughput (payload 8 B-512 MiB, message rate and bitrate) and 64 B ping-pong latency (RTT/2), single machine (localhost) and 3 machines on 100GbE. Cyclone DDS runs peer-to-peer with test programs based on the official roundtrip example (RELIABLE, KEEP_ALL for throughput). Kafka runs a single 3.2.1 broker with the rust-rdkafka 0.28.0 client, tuned with linger.ms=0, acks=0, compression none and batch.size 400KB (throughput) / 1 (latency).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 1.3k stars; a qualified Tier-1 ROS 2 RMW implementation shipped with ROS 2 (per the paper)
corrections.caveats: arXiv v1 preprint, not peer-reviewed. The benchmark code it cites (github.com/ZettaScaleLabs/zenoh-perf, comparison/cyclonedds and comparison/kafka) now returns 404, so the results cannot be reproduced from public code. No compiler or flags are stated. The authors are the ZettaScale Zenoh team plus NTU. ZettaScale was then the main Cyclone DDS developer: 45 of the last 100 default-branch commits before June 2023 came from zettascale.tech addresses. The comparison is therefore not arm's-length for Cyclone DDS. It is also not like-for-like: DDS runs brokerless peer-to-peer (UDP multicast), while Kafka goes through a single broker with no durability (acks=0), and Kafka is a persistent log that DDS does not replace. The Rust Kafka binding failed above 1 MB, so Kafka was not measured above 512 KiB. The software is from 2023 (Kafka 3.2.1).

notes: The numbers match the paper, but the record's claim that the harness is public is false (zenoh-perf is 404 on both the GitHub API and github.com), and so is its claim that the authors are not Cyclone DDS maintainers. I re-derived the ratios from the appendix raw tables at matched payload sizes. The license is EDL-1.0, which is BSD-3-Clause (NOTICE.md gives the SPDX expression EPL-2.0 OR BSD-3-Clause). The head commit's author date is 2026-09-21 and its committer date is 2026-09-25. I could not verify the 'default ROS 2 RMW' wording, because both ROS docs pages I tried returned 404, so usage is now phrased as the paper states it.

tier_reason: This is the same arXiv 2303.09419 v1 preprint, measuring Mosquitto 2.0.15 with the Paho C client against Kafka 3.2.1. The CPU is stated, but there is no compiler or flags, the cited benchmark code (ZettaScaleLabs/zenoh-perf, comparison/mqtt) is 404, and the paper is not peer-reviewed. It is a Zenoh vendor study rather than an established independent suite, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Latency (64 B ping-pong, RTT/2), per Tab. 2/3: MQTT 27 us vs Kafka 73 us on a single machine (~2.7x), and 45 us vs 84 us multi-machine (~1.9x) (derived from page data). The throughput win is narrow. On a single machine at 32 KiB, MQTT gets 7.6 Gbps vs Kafka's 3.6 Gbps (~2.1x); at 16 KiB it is 4.8 vs 4.2 Gbps (~1.1x) (derived from page data, Tab. 5). Multi-machine at 32 KiB it is 8.6 vs 4.6 Gbps (~1.9x) (derived from page data, Tab. 7). Kafka wins elsewhere: message rate at 8 B is 61.6K vs 34.2K msg/s (~1.8x in Kafka's favour), and at 64 KiB Kafka reaches 3.6 Gbps vs MQTT's 222 Mbps (~16x in Kafka's favour) (derived from page data).

notes: The record's figures are right, but its claim that the harness is public is false: zenoh-perf returns 404. The paper's prose swaps the two latencies ('MQTT and Kafka have a latency of 73 us and 27 us, respectively'), but Tab. 2 gives Kafka 73 and MQTT 27, which the record correctly follows. The metric field says throughput, but the more robust win is latency, which holds in both scenarios; the throughput win exists only at 16-32 KiB. The license is EDL-1.0, which is BSD-3-Clause (LICENSE.txt SPDX: EPL-2.0 OR BSD-3-Clause), and the last commit (2026-09-03) and stars (11.2k) check out.

tier_reason: The paper (arXiv 2508.07934) was peer-reviewed and published at IEEE SRDS 2025 (DOI 10.1109/SRDS69199.2025.00036). It is an independent Hitachi Energy study of NanoMsg vs ZeroMQ (and NNG) that states the CPU (Xeon w3-2435) and publishes its code and raw data in hitachienergy/messaging-libraries-benchmark: bml/pub-sub.c, bml/ops_nanomsg.c, bml/ops_zeromq.c, results/runner.sh and results/results.csv. It is not A: the harness is built with gcc -O2 (bml/Makefile) but the gcc version is unstated, and the libraries under test are prebuilt distro apt packages whose distro release, compiler and flags are never stated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: The paper states the win qualitatively and gives no ratios. NanoMsg has the lowest average latency of ZeroMQ, NanoMsg and NNG for payloads up to 64 KB In-Process and up to 128 KB Inter-Process (Obs. 1, 2, 4). It also has the lowest CPU at every size Inter-Process (Obs. 5) and the lowest memory (Obs. 11). The margin is modest. With 1 subscriber and a 1000 us publish interval, average latency at 1 KB is 7.5 us vs ZeroMQ's 10.3 us In-Process (~1.4x) and 16.2 vs 25.8 us Inter-Process (~1.6x), shrinking to ~1.1-1.2x at 32 KB (derived from the paper's artifact results/results.csv). Over TCP, NanoMsg leads only up to 8 KB (~1.2x) and is far slower than ZeroMQ at 16-32 KB (about 560 us vs 40 us, derived from the same CSV). ZeroMQ wins peak throughput (~4.8 vs ~3.8 GB/s In-Process; ~2.9 GB/s IPC/TCP), large-payload latency and throughput scaling with more subscribers.
corrections.workload: Brokerless PUB/SUB with all processes on one host, over In-Process, Inter-Process (IPC) and TCP-loopback transports. Payload runs from 1 KB to 512 KB in powers of two (x1000 B) with 1 subscriber, and 1/2/4/8 subscribers are tested at 32 KB. Each run sends C=5000 messages after a 1000 ms publisher delay, averaged over R=4 runs. Latency uses a 1000 us publish interval and throughput/CPU use 0 us. Versions: ZeroMQ (libzmq 4.3.4 + CZMQ 4.2.1), NanoMsg 1.1.5 and NNG 1.9.0.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: The harness (bml/) is built with gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 (bml/Makefile); the gcc version is not stated. ZeroMQ/CZMQ and NanoMsg come from distro apt packages (libzmq3-dev, libczmq-dev, libnanomsg-dev), with the distro release and build flags not stated. NNG 1.9.0 is built from source with CMake/Ninja defaults.
corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed (IEEE SRDS 2025; arXiv 2508.07934 is the preprint), independent of all three projects, with open MIT-licensed code and raw results (github.com/hitachienergy/messaging-libraries-benchmark). The compiler version and the libraries' build flags are not stated (distro packages), which keeps it off tier A. The latency win is modest (~1.1-1.6x) and holds only for small-to-medium payloads. ZeroMQ wins peak throughput, large payloads and subscriber scaling, and over TCP NanoMsg has a severe latency anomaly at 16-64 KB. The tested nanomsg 1.1.5 is old. Both the paper and the nanomsg README say the library is in 'sustaining' mode: new feature work has ended, only severe bugs get fixed, and new projects are pointed to NNG. All runs used one host, 5000 messages x 4 runs.

notes: The record's claim is accurate in substance. I added magnitudes from the artifact CSV (clearly labelled) and the TCP caveat. The tier stays B, but for a stronger reason than the record gave: the paper is peer-reviewed at SRDS 2025, not just an arXiv preprint. Metadata checks out: MIT license (COPYING is the Expat text; the GitHub API reports NOASSERTION), last commit 2026-09-06, 6.3k stars, not archived. 'Active' follows the commit-date rule even though the project calls itself sustaining.
